doc.title: Jamey Aebersold interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 26, 2022

title: Teaching the eighth graders: swing, legato and practice
summary: Students feel the swing, are told not to tongue, jazz still scares people, and kids start practicing.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Do you have to, do you find it necessary to try to explain and/or demonstrate the difference between swing and straight, or do they do it pretty much because of the way the song sounds?

Yeah. That’s a good question. They have not listened to any jazz at all but I will say this, the first time I put a CD on the baritone player and Sebastian, the tenor player next to him, they’re snapping on two and four. And today they were doing that while everybody was soloing, even though it was a bossa nova. So they can feel this music. And when we start to play, going back a month, they tongued everything. So I had to tell them to stop tonguing, play legato. And of course I had my sax and I would demonstrate it. And they seemed to be picking things up. Now I haven’t said “Don’t tongue” in a long time. I said

it today when we did the minor scale, just to be safe ‘cause this was a new scale and they’re having trouble figuring the lowered third and lowered seventh. But they all sound pretty good. And we played a blues last week and they — but they’re not swinging. Well I guess they were swinging, because two adult teachers came in the door and were smiling, “Hey what are you all doing?” I said, “We’re trying to swing.” “Well it sure sounds good out here to us.” Which I’m sure made the kids feel good. But we haven’t really entered into the swing yet because we haven’t played — it’s just not there yet.
You said the next — this upcoming engagement you’re going south for, you made this little aside saying I don’t know how they’re going to bill it. If they bill it as jazz no one will come.

If they bill it as jazz then there’ll probably be twelve or thirteen jazzers there. But the violins won’t come, the oboes, the trumpets that don’t [inaudible] in the orchestra. This jazz thing, Monk, is still really scary to so many people. Oh it’s just — and it’s so silly because I can get them playing in no time at all. I was with somebody the other day who is a professional and his playing doesn’t swing. Okay? But he doesn’t really play swing stuff but there was someone playing with him that I know and he was talking to me about this fellow’s playing. And I told him, I said, “Well if I could somehow get together with this fellow for an hour I think I could straighten him out, because there are certain things in his lines that are not proper. The phrases aren’t ending right, even though he’s an adult and has been playing for a long time.” When I hear him play it’s all detached like. And I’ve discovered how to un-detach it and make it singable and make the phrases go like that. And if you start that early, which I’m trying to do with these kids, then I think it’s going to — once they ever decide to get into it and start practicing — hey that’s another thing. I told their teacher a week ago I said, “These kids are not practicing at all. I’m wasting my time.” Next day I come to class, I get there early. We’ve got a little gym room and chairs and stands are all set up. And I get in there, I’m in there ten minutes and I look at my phone, what’s going on? I said uh oh, she is giving them a lecture about practicing. Not the eight kids, but the eight kids and the other forty kids that are in the eighth grade band. I walk in and sure enough, she’s really a good teacher. So this past weekend, just now, Lillian, Lilly, the girl, saxophone player, she said, “I practiced an hour and a half on Friday.” Hallelujah. You know? And the little boy over here said, Xavier, he said, “I practiced two and a half hours over the weekend.” He’s been into it. He’s the only one with the CD player so I gave him Volume 1 and I gave him Volume 54, and I gave him Volume 24. He’s practicing.
